title: Being who you are, while becoming better: feed the motor, manage its side effects
summary: Jason Cohen argues that "be yourself" must include being a person who strives and keeps improving. He uses his own fight with procrastination to show why you shouldn't just accept faults. He also lists the common entrepreneur side effects of that internal "motor" and how to manage them.

principles.text: Being yourself includes being someone who strives. Don't accept faults as fixed; keep improving who you are.
principles.quote: I've decided to continue to the fight, because I know something else about "who I am"--I'm a person who strives.

principles.text: Successful entrepreneurs have an internal 'motor' that compels them to keep building, which is why serial entrepreneurs repeat.
principles.quote: You do the third one for the same reason you did the first one--because you are *compelled* to.

principles.text: Procrastination excuses sound logical but are bullshit. Time exists; you're choosing to spend it elsewhere, so delegate or delete instead.
principles.quote: Time always exists, you're deciding to do something else with that time.

principles.text: Be the best at one thing and keep improving at the rest, rather than needing to beat everyone at everything.
principles.quote: the new challenge was to (1) be the best at *one thing* (telling a computer what to do), and (2) be constantly improving in other things.

principles.text: Manage the motor's side effects (spread too thin, shiny-new-thing, overwork, perfectionism) by acknowledging them and saying no to new projects.
principles.quote: Learn to say "no" to new projects (allowing you to continue a healthy obsession over a few).

principles.text: Decide what you believe and run your company accordingly and publicly, rather than writing empty marketing prose; never compromise ethics or taste.
principles.quote: decide what you believe, then run your company accordingly and publicly and you *will* be more proud, more fulfilled, and likely more successful.
